aliases: Jiang Mu Xiang ginger aroma Dan Cong
processing: Made the way Phoenix dancong usually is: sun-withered, shaken and rested in rounds until the leaf edges redden, then fixed, rolled and dried. Roast level varies by maker.
harvest_season: As with most Phoenix dancong, the spring picking is the main and most prized one; dates for this line are not well documented.
appearance_dry: Long, twisted strands in dark brown to grey-brown, as is typical of Phoenix dancong, though the ginger-flower lines are described as a little shorter than most.
appearance_liquor: Clear golden yellow, typical of ginger-flower dancong.
appearance_wet: Long leaves with reddened edges, as is usual for well-shaken dancong.
taste_profile: Sweet and brisk with a faint ginger heat in the mouth, which is what gives it its name. Ginger-flower aroma sits on top of it.

brewing.notes: General dancong approach: very hot water and fast pours. Long steeps turn dancong bitter quickly, and that bitterness would cover the ginger note.

vintage_note: No selling pattern specific to this line is documented. Like other Phoenix dancong it is normally sold by spring harvest of the current year, often after a roast and a rest of some months, and older roasted stock is sold with its year stated. It is described as a rare line, so ask a seller which village and tree the leaf comes from.
description:
Jiang Mu Xiang is a Phoenix Mountain dancong named for 'mother ginger', the old, hot rhizome. The point of the tea is a faint ginger bite running through an otherwise sweet, brisk cup.

It belongs to the ginger-flower aroma family, one of the ten aroma types people use to sort dancong, and it also goes by Tong Tian Xiang. Accounts differ on how tight that equation is: some treat the two names as one tea, while at least one vendor's list of Phoenix trees gives Jiang Mu Xiang and Tong Tian Xiang as separate entries in the same family.

Processing notes for this line are scarce, so expect what is typical of dancong: long shaking and resting, then a drying or roast that decides how bright the aroma stays. Brew it hot and quick, as you would any dancong; the ginger comes through best when the steep is short.

It is a rare line and the name is easy to attach to any ginger-flower tea. A seller who can tell you the village is a better sign than the label. Taste it next to a plain Jiang Hua Xiang to learn what the family has in common.
history:
Little is documented about when this line was selected. Chinese tea writing gives Jiang Mu Cha as its older name and Tong Tian Xiang as a later one, and explains the name by the slight ginger heat of the liquor.

One vendor's list of Phoenix trees places a Jiang Mu Xiang mother tree in Zhongping, Fengxi Village, at about 900 m and about 200 years old; that is a seller's figure, not a surveyed one.
